title: 39. Effects of an antibody-based direct-fed microbial on feed intake, growth performance, and feed efficiency in feedlot cattle.
content:
Abstract
This study evaluated whether an antibody-based direct-fed microbial alters feed intake, growth performance, and feed efficiency in finishing beef cattle. The product is marketed to improve performance in finishing cattle through modulation of ruminal microbial activity, with the intent of increasing growth rate and feed efficiency. A total of 160 steers (initial body weight = 469 ± 30 kg) were used in a randomized complete block design, with pen serving as the experimental unit. Steers were stratified by source, blocked by initial body weight, and assigned to one of two treatments: a control diet or a diet supplemented with an antibody-based direct-fed microbial. Cattle were housed at the Kansas State University Agricultural Research Center feedlot in Hays, KS, and were fed for 84 days. Steers were allocated to eight pens (n = 4 per treatment), with 20 steers per pen. Within each treatment, pens were further blocked by weight, consisting of two heavy and two light pens. Cattle were weighed individually at 28-day intervals to determine average daily gain. Performance variables measured included dry matter intake (DMI), average daily gain (ADG), total body weight gain, and gain-to-feed ratio (G:F). Dry matter intake was calculated on a pen basis as the total feed delivered divided by the number of animals per pen. Data were analyzed using the PROC MIXED procedure of SAS (version 9.4), with treatment included as a fixed effect and block included as a random effect. No differences were observed between treatments for G:F (P = 0.61), ADG (P = 0.36), or total body weight gain (P = 0.78). However, dry matter intake differed between treatments (P < 0.0001), with control cattle consuming more feed (15 kg/hd/d) than cattle receiving the antibody-based direct-fed microbial (14 kg/hd/d). These results indicate that although the antibody-based direct-fed microbial reduced feed intake, it did not negatively impact growth performance or feed efficiency in finishing beef cattle under the conditions of this study.
